question: The soldiers fought <u>out</u> when attacked by the enemies.
explanation: 'Fight back' means to defend oneself against an attack, which fits 'when attacked by the enemies'. 'Fight on' (keep fighting) is also acceptable. 'Fought out' does not mean resisting an attack.

question: We should have the courage to fight <u>with</u> our rights.
explanation: 'Fight for' means to struggle to defend or win something. 'Fight with' means to fight alongside someone or against a person, so it does not suit 'our rights'.

question: The tickets for the new Avengers movie were sold <u>away</u> within a few hours.
explanation: 'Sold out' means the whole stock has been sold and none is left. 'Sold away' is not used in this sense.

question: The chef was eager to sell <u>out</u> the last of the cakes.
explanation: 'Sell off' means to sell the remaining stock quickly, often cheaply. 'Sell out' does not take an object like this; it describes stock that is completely sold, or means to betray.

question: The grandmother promised to bring <u>about</u> the children well.
explanation: 'Bring up' means to raise and educate a child. 'Bring about' means to cause something to happen.

question: The new principal said he would bring <u>on</u> many changes.
explanation: 'Bring about' means to cause changes to happen, and 'bring in' means to introduce them. 'Bring on' means to cause something unpleasant, such as an illness, so it does not fit.

question: Although she faced a tragedy, we are sure she will get <u>off</u> it soon.
explanation: 'Get over' means to recover from an illness, shock or sad experience.

question: At the end of the year, we all want to get <u>out</u> from the hustle and bustle of the city.
explanation: 'Get away from' means to escape from or take a break from a place or situation.

question: Be sure to put <u>out</u> your lifejacket before you get onboard.
explanation: 'Put on' means to wear a piece of clothing or equipment. 'Put out' means to extinguish (a fire) or to place something outside.

question: She refused to put <u>on</u> with their antics any more.
explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate something annoying.

question: She was let <u>away</u> with a warning as her actions were not deliberate.
explanation: 'Let off' means to allow someone to go without punishment, or with a light one.

question: The rain did not let <u>on</u> so they were forced to cancel the plan for a picnic.
explanation: 'Let up' means to stop or become less intense, usually said of rain or pressure. 'Let on' means to reveal a secret.

question: When he got his birthday cake, he blew <u>off</u> all the candles on it.
explanation: 'Blow out' means to extinguish a flame by blowing.

question: They had to take shelter for the night till the storm blew <u>away</u>.
explanation: 'Blow over' means that a storm or trouble passes without lasting effect.

question: She always brought <u>on</u> the best in her students.
explanation: 'Bring out' means to cause a quality or ability to show itself.

question: The guests were cautioned not to bring <u>about</u> the sensitive topic.
explanation: 'Bring up' means to raise a subject for discussion.

question: Their plans fell <u>off</u> due to disagreements in the team.
explanation: 'Fall through' means that a plan fails or does not happen. 'Fall apart' also fits (the plans collapsed). 'Fall off' means to drop or decrease.

question: They have not spoken to each other since they fallen <u>away</u> many years ago.
explanation: 'Fall out' means to quarrel and stop being friends. (Note: the printed sentence has a grammatical slip, 'they fallen' instead of 'they fell' or 'they had fallen'.)

question: The boy takes <u>over</u> his father in every way.
explanation: 'Take after' means to resemble an older family member in looks or character. 'Take over' means to assume control.

question: I took <u>on</u> swimming quicker than my parents thought I would.
explanation: 'Take to' means to begin to like something or find it easy. 'Take on' means to accept a task or challenge.

question: The lyrics had been put <u>for</u> music.
explanation: 'Put to music' means to set words to a tune.

question: His indifferent attitude has put us <u>in</u>.
explanation: 'Put off' means to discourage or repel someone.

question: The disgraced minister fell <u>for</u> power.
explanation: 'Fall from power' means to lose a position of authority. 'Fall for' means to fall in love with or be tricked by.

question: New Year’s Day falls <u>in</u> a Tuesday this year.
explanation: 'Fall on' is used for dates that coincide with a day of the week.

question: The candidate’s name was struck <u>away</u> the rolls on his request.
explanation: 'Strike off' means to remove a name from an official list.

question: I was struck <u>with</u> the startling resemblance between the mother and the daughter.
explanation: 'Be struck by' means to be strongly impressed by something. 'By' is the standard preposition here.

question: The judge was bowled <u>away</u> by the talent of the students at the fest.
explanation: 'Bowled over' means overwhelmed with surprise or admiration.

question: The player was declared bowled <u>over</u> by the umpire.
explanation: 'Bowled out' is the cricket term for a batsman dismissed when the ball hits the stumps.

question: Maanya was able to deal <u>away</u> the delicate situation.
explanation: 'Deal with' means to handle or manage a situation.

question: Mr Lakhmani deals <u>with</u> antiques and curios.
explanation: 'Deal in' means to buy and sell a type of goods.

question: Vansh keeps putting <u>on</u> going to the dentist.
explanation: 'Put off' means to postpone.

question: They offered to put us <u>in</u> for the night when we visited their city.
explanation: 'Put up' means to give someone a place to stay.

question: It is a good idea to back <u>on</u> your files onto a memory stick.
explanation: 'Back up' means to make a copy of data as a precaution.

question: He lost confidence and backed <u>off</u> of the deal at the last minute.
explanation: 'Back out of' means to withdraw from an agreement or commitment. ('Back off' means to retreat and is not idiomatic with 'of the deal'.)

question: It was cloudy since morning but the sun finally broke <u>over</u> the clouds at noon.
explanation: 'Break through' means to emerge from behind or force a way through an obstacle.

question: The burglars broke <u>through</u> the store after midnight.
explanation: 'Break into' means to enter a building by force.

question: It is time to fight <u>with</u> street crime.
explanation: 'Fight against' means to oppose or combat something harmful.

question: He was hurt while trying to fight <u>away</u> the robbers.
explanation: 'Fight off' means to drive away an attacker by fighting.

question: The doctors think that she will pull <u>away</u>.
explanation: 'Pull through' means to recover from a serious illness or difficulty.

question: No one expected him to pull <u>on</u> a trick like that.
explanation: 'Pull off' means to succeed in doing something difficult or unexpected.

question: The coach called <u>away</u> the training session due to heavy rain.
explanation: 'Call off' means to cancel.

question: We decided to call <u>out</u> our aunt who lived in a nearby city.
explanation: 'Call on' means to visit someone, and 'call up' means to telephone them. Both fit. 'Call out' means to shout or summon.

question: While looking through the old album, I came <u>to</u> a funny picture of mine.
explanation: 'Come across' means to find something by chance.

question: The food in this restaurant is so good that we will surely come <u>up</u> for more.
explanation: 'Come back for more' means to return in order to get more of something.
